mex_001: You can recognise it by its immense trunk, over 18 metres round, the thickest protected tree in the city, its crown lower since a 2018 storm broke part of it away. It stands in the small Plazuela de San Juan Bautista in Xochimilco.
mex_002: You can recognise it by its huge cypress trunk, nearly 14 metres round, under a crown reaching 27 metres. It stands beside the Santa Catarina Martir parish church, behind the primary school in Azcapotzalco.
mex_003: You can recognise it by its wide fig crown, close to 20 metres across, shading the whole street corner. It stands on the pavement where Miguel Laurent meets Calle Fresas in Tlacoquemecatl del Valle.
mex_005: You can recognise it by its straight, century-old cypress trunk, just over 5 metres round and about 28 metres tall. It stands inside Parque Espana in Roma Norte, planted the day the park opened in 1921.
mex_006: You can recognise it by its broad crown, about 22 metres wide, inside the small Jardin de San Fernando. It stands beside, but is not part of, the separate, ticketed Panteon de San Fernando cemetery next door.
mex_007: You can recognise it by its huge trunk, just over 10 metres round, rising from an ordinary pavement corner. It stands where Avenida Marina Nacional meets Golfo de Bengala in Tacuba, streets from the ruined Arbol de la Noche Triste.
mex_008: You can recognise it by its base, two great stems about 1.5 and 1.6 metres across rising together, easy to mistake for one trunk. It stands in the public park wrapping the old convent walls at Churubusco.
mex_009: You can recognise it by its lone trunk, 5.65 metres round, standing on the median strip of Callejon del Rio. It marks the old course of the Rio Magdalena in Coyoacan, about 700 metres from the Francisco Sosa ash.
mex_010: You can recognise it by its huge, almost round crown, 26 metres across, unusual for a street ash. It stands on the pavement outside number 202, Avenida Francisco Sosa, in Coyoacan.
